summary: Defines the Assured Forwarding group of Differentiated Services behaviors. It offers several traffic classes, each with different levels of how likely a packet is to be dropped when a router is congested. It lets operators give some traffic better odds of delivery than other traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a crowded bus where some passengers hold gold tickets. If the bus gets too full, people with plain tickets are asked to step off first.

subtitle: Four forwarding classes, three drop precedences each: how a congested router decides whose packets to discard first.

tldr.problem: A customer wants its IP traffic delivered with high probability as long as it stays within a subscribed rate, while traffic above that rate may be delivered with lower probability. Packets of the same flow must also not be reordered.
tldr.mechanism: The Assured Forwarding (AF) group defines four independently forwarded classes, each with three drop precedence levels. Under congestion a node discards higher drop precedence packets first, using a queue management algorithm with gradual, flow-insensitive dropping.
tldr.outcome: The RFC fixes the behavior, 12 recommended codepoints and the rules for coexisting with other PHBs, but leaves the exact algorithm and resource allocation to implementers. RFC 3260 later updated it.

today: RFC 2597 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 3260; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Purpose and Overview
sections.content:
The motivating case is a company that uses the Internet to link its distributed sites. It wants an assurance that packets are forwarded with high probability as long as the traffic from each site stays within the subscribed information rate (the profile). Sending more than the profile should be allowed, with the understanding that the excess is delivered with lower probability. The network must also avoid reordering packets of the same microflow, whether they are in or out of profile.

Assured Forwarding (AF) is a Differentiated Services (DS) per-hop behavior group that lets a provider DS domain offer different levels of forwarding assurance for packets received from a customer DS domain. Four AF classes are defined, and each class is allocated a certain amount of buffer space and bandwidth in each DS node. Within a class, packets carry one of three drop precedence values. In congestion, a node tries to protect lower drop precedence packets by discarding higher drop precedence packets first.

The assurance a packet gets thus depends on three things: the resources allocated to its class, the current load of that class, and, during congestion within the class, its drop precedence. A DS-compliant node is not required to implement the AF group, but a node that claims to implement it must follow this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The network offers four lanes, and in each lane some packets wear a badge saying how important they are. When a lane jams, the least important badges get dropped first.

sections.title: The AF PHB Group
sections.content:
The group is defined with N classes and M drop precedence levels. A packet in class i with drop precedence j is marked with the codepoint AFij. For general use, N=4 and M=3. More classes or levels MAY be defined for local use.

A DS node SHOULD implement all four general use classes, and it MUST forward packets of different classes independently, never aggregating two or more classes together. It MUST give each implemented class a configurable minimum of buffer space and bandwidth, and each class SHOULD be serviced to achieve the configured rate over both small and large time scales. A class MAY be configurable to receive more than its minimum when spare resources exist. The RFC does not say how, but implementations MUST document which algorithms they support and how they are parameterized.

Within a class, a node MUST NOT forward a packet with drop precedence p with smaller probability than one with drop precedence q when p < q. A node MUST accept all three drop precedence codepoints and they MUST yield at least two different levels of loss probability. Two levels may be reasonable where congestion is rare and brief, such as some enterprise networks, but three levels SHOULD be supported where congestion is common. With only two levels, AFx1 MUST give the lower loss probability and AFx2 and AFx3 the higher.

A node MUST NOT reorder AF packets of the same microflow in the same class, whatever their drop precedence. There are no quantifiable delay or delay variation requirements for AF packets.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four separate lanes that never get mixed together. In each lane, packets marked low, medium or high are dropped in the order high, medium, low when things get crowded, and packets in a line keep their order.

sections.title: Traffic Conditioning, Queueing and Discard
sections.content:
A DS domain MAY condition AF traffic at its edge: shaping it, discarding packets, raising or lowering drop precedence, or moving packets to other AF classes. These actions MUST NOT reorder packets of the same microflow. When AF packets are tunneled, the tunnel's PHB MUST NOT reduce the forwarding assurance of the tunneled packet or reorder packets of the same microflow.

An AF implementation MUST try to minimize long-term congestion within each class while allowing short-term bursts. That calls for an active queue management algorithm, with Random Early Drop (RED) given as an example, though no particular algorithm is required. The node MUST respond to long-term congestion by dropping, and absorb short-term bursts by queueing, which implies a smoothed congestion level computed from the instantaneous one.

The dropping algorithm MUST be insensitive to short-term traffic characteristics: flows with different burst shapes but identical longer-term packet rates should see essentially equal discard probability. It MUST treat all packets of one class and precedence level identically. The feedback to end nodes MUST be gradual rather than abrupt so the system can reach a stable operating point. In the RED example, no packets are discarded below a first threshold, the discard probability rises linearly between two thresholds, and above the second threshold packets of that precedence are discarded with 100% probability. The control parameters MUST be independently configurable for each drop precedence and each AF class.

The RFC admits that allowing a range of discard behaviors can lead to inconsistent end-to-end service in multi-vendor networks, and says future versions may define the behavior more tightly.
sections.plainLanguage: The edge of the network can sort and slow down traffic before it enters. Inside, a router starts dropping a few packets early and gently as a line grows, rather than waiting until it is totally full, so everyone slows down smoothly.

sections.title: Recommended Codepoints
sections.content:
The RECOMMENDED codepoints for the four general use classes are AF11 = 001010, AF12 = 001100, AF13 = 001110, AF21 = 010010, AF22 = 010100, AF23 = 010110, AF31 = 011010, AF32 = 011100, AF33 = 011110, AF41 = 100010, AF42 = 100100 and AF43 = 100110. They do not overlap with any other general use PHB group.

The first digit of the AF name is the class and the second is the drop precedence: 1 is low, 2 is medium and 3 is high. These twelve codepoints are allocated in Pool 1 of the code space defined by RFC 2474, which is the IANA action in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Each badge is a short six-digit code of ones and zeros. The RFC hands out twelve of them, one for each lane and importance level.

sections.title: Interaction with Other PHB Groups
sections.content:
The AF codepoints do not interfere with the local use spaces or the Class Selector codepoints of RFC 2474, so those PHBs can coexist with AF. The Default PHB codepoint 000000 may stay in use for best effort traffic, and 11x000 for network control traffic. With edge conditioning that limits each class to a percentage of its resources, AF can reproduce the behavior implied by the Class Selector PHBs, and Class Selector codepoints may then serve as aliases of AF codepoints.

Any AF implementation should document two things. First, which other PHB groups may preempt resources allocated to an AF class. This MUST NOT happen in normal operation, but the 11x000 network control codepoint may do so when control traffic is unexpectedly high. Second, how excess resources are shared between AF and other PHB groups. The RFC requires only that the chosen relationship be documented, and implementations MAY make it configurable.
sections.plainLanguage: The new badges do not clash with older ones. If the bus driver needs to let an emergency crew on, they may take a seat, but the rule has to be written down.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
To protect itself from denial of service attacks, a provider DS domain SHOULD limit the traffic entering it to the subscribed profiles. To protect the link to a customer domain, it SHOULD let the customer specify how the link's resources are allocated to AF packets. If a service restricts AF-marked traffic by attributes such as source or destination address, the ingress node is responsible for verifying those attributes.

Other security considerations are covered in RFC 2475 and RFC 2474.
sections.plainLanguage: The bus company should only let people on according to the tickets they bought, so that nobody can crowd out everyone else.

sections.title: Example Services
sections.content:
The appendix sketches how AF could be used. One example is an Olympic service with bronze, silver and gold classes, mapped to AF classes 1, 2 and 3, where gold sees lighter load than silver and silver lighter than bronze. Low, medium and high drop precedence map to AF levels 1, 2 and 3.

Drop precedence could be assigned by a leaky bucket policer with a rate and a size that is the sum of a committed burst size and an excess burst size. A packet gets low drop precedence if the bucket holds more tokens than the excess burst size, medium if it holds some tokens but at most the excess burst size, and high if the bucket is empty. The RFC suggests capping the amount of high drop precedence traffic a customer domain may send, so it cannot deny service to other domains.

AF could also provide a proportional bandwidth service, or a low loss and low latency service using an over-provisioned class. Without over-provisioning, low latency can be had by setting a low maximum buffer limit for a class. The admission control such services need is outside this document.
sections.plainLanguage: A water bucket fills with tokens as you send. If you have plenty of water you get the top badge, a little gets the middle badge, and an empty bucket gets the lowest badge.

viz.caption: WHAT A NODE MUST DO FOR AF

items.title: Classes stay separate
items.text: Packets in one AF class are forwarded independently of the other classes.

items.title: Minimum resources
items.text: Each implemented class gets a configurable minimum of buffer space and bandwidth.

items.title: Drop order
items.text: Higher drop precedence never gets a better forwarding chance than lower within a class.

items.title: No reordering
items.text: Packets of one microflow in one class are never reordered.
